title: render_partial()
text:
Render a partial template to an HTML fragment.


Usage
Source


render_partial(template_file, **template_data)


Looks up template_file in the folder registered with register_extensions and renders it with the supplied keyword arguments as its model. render_partial is injected into the model automatically, so a partial can render further nested partials. The fragment is rendered as text (str); any bytes values in the model are decoded as UTF-8.


Parameters


template_file: str

Path to the partial, relative to the registered templates folder, for example shared/partials/video_image.pt.

**template_data: Any

Keyword arguments passed to the template as its model (the variables the template can reference). Values may be any Python objects your template expressions use. The name encoding is reserved and cannot be used; translate, target_language, and repeat have special meaning to Chameleon.





Returns


 HTML

An HTML wrapper whose __html__ method yields the rendered markup as safe, pre-escaped HTML.





Raises


 PartialsException

If register_extensions has not been called yet.

 ValueError

Raised as Chameleon raises it for a missing file (Template not found: ...) when template_file does not name a regular file under the registered folder: a missing file, a folder, or a name that would reach outside the folder (an absolute path, a .. out of the folder, or a package:path spec).





Note
Surrounding whitespace is stripped and ./, //, and a .. that stays inside the folder are normalized away, so every spelling of a file compiles and caches one template. Distinct case spellings on a case-insensitive filesystem (macOS, Windows) still cache separately. The check that keeps a name inside the folder is lexical, so a symlink inside the folder is still followed.
Choose the partial in your code, never from request data. If a request picks the fragment, map the request value to a name you wrote (PARTIALS = {'card': 'partials/card.pt'}) instead of building the path from it, and pass the model as named keyword arguments rather than spreading a request’s parameters into it (render_partial(name, **request.params) lets a parameter replace a name the template relies on, such as render_partial itself).


Examples
import chameleon_partials

chameleon_partials.register_extensions('path/to/templates')
html = chameleon_partials.render_partial('shared/partials/user_card.pt', name='Sarah', age=32)
print(html.html_text)

title: extend_model()
text:
Add render_partial to a view model so templates can call it.


Usage
Source


extend_model(model)


Use this in frameworks where a view returns a model dictionary (for example FastAPI) and you need render_partial available inside the template. For Pyramid, prefer the BeforeRender middleware shown in the README instead. Any existing render_partial key in the model is replaced.


Parameters


model: Optional[Dict[str, Any]]

The view model dictionary to extend. None is treated as an empty model.





Returns


 Dict[str, Any]

The same dictionary with a render_partial key added, or a new dictionary when model is None.





Raises


 PartialsException

If model is not a dictionary (and not None).





Examples
import chameleon_partials

model = {'name': 'Sarah'}
model = chameleon_partials.extend_model(model)
# model['render_partial'] is now callable from the template.

title: PartialsException
text:
Raised when chameleon_partials is configured or used incorrectly.


Usage
Source


PartialsException()


Examples include registering with a missing template folder, rendering a partial before calling register_extensions, or passing a non-dictionary model to extend_model. Errors raised by Chameleon itself, such as the ValueError for a missing template file, are propagated unchanged rather than wrapped in this type.


Examples
import chameleon_partials

try:
    chameleon_partials.render_partial('shared/partials/user_card.pt', name='Sarah')
except chameleon_partials.PartialsException:
    # register_extensions() has not been called yet; do that at startup.
    raise
except ValueError:
    # Chameleon's own error: the template file is missing or outside the folder.
    raise

SKILL.md
---
name: chameleon-partials
description: >-
  Renders reusable HTML fragments (partials) inside Chameleon templates for any Python web framework that renders Chameleon, such as Pyramid or FastAPI. Use when adding chameleon_partials to an app, calling render_partial from a .pt template or from Python, wiring render_partial into Pyramid (BeforeRender) or another framework (extend_model), testing partials with pytest, or fixing PartialsException, ValueError "Template not found", NameError: render_partial, escaped markup, or template edits that do not show up.
license: MIT
compatibility: Requires Python >=3.10 and Chameleon. Framework-agnostic; the example app uses Pyramid.
---

# chameleon-partials

Chameleon has no built-in way to reuse a fragment of HTML across pages. chameleon_partials adds `render_partial(path, **model)`: a template calls it inside `${ }` to insert a fragment template from a folder registered once at startup, passing keyword arguments as the fragment's model. It returns an `HTML` object, not a `str`, which Chameleon inserts unescaped through `__html__`. Misuse raises `PartialsException`; a missing or refused template raises Chameleon's own `ValueError` (`Template not found: ...`).

## Install

`uv add chameleon-partials` or `pip install chameleon-partials`. The import name is `chameleon_partials`.

## Use

```python
# Application startup, once, before any template renders.
from pathlib import Path
import chameleon_partials

folder = (Path(__file__).parent / 'templates').as_posix()
chameleon_partials.register_extensions(folder, auto_reload=dev_mode)  # auto_reload=False in production
```

```html
<!-- Any page template or partial. The path is relative to the registered folder. -->
<span tal:repeat="v videos">${ render_partial('shared/partials/video_square.pt', video=v) }</span>
```

Pyramid: add a `BeforeRender` subscriber in a package that `config.scan()` covers, and every template gets `render_partial`:

```python
from pyramid.events import BeforeRender, subscriber
import chameleon_partials


@subscriber(BeforeRender)
def add_global(event):
    event['render_partial'] = chameleon_partials.render_partial
```

Other frameworks: `return chameleon_partials.extend_model(model)` from the view. Tests: register the test template folder in a fixture, set `chameleon_partials.has_registered_extensions = False` in its teardown, and assert on `render_partial(...).html_text`.

## Rules

- Partial paths are always relative to the registered folder, never to the calling template, even inside a nested partial. Chameleon's `metal:use-macro="load: ../shared/_layout.pt"` is relative to the current file. Do not mix the two rules.
- `register_extensions` does nothing after one successful call (default `cache_init=True`). To re-point it, pass `cache_init=False` or reset `has_registered_extensions`. A call that raised did not register, so fix the folder and call again.
- Registration is module-global and not lock-guarded: call it from startup code, not from request handlers. Rendering after registration is safe from several threads.
- `PartialsException` means misuse only: rendering before registration, an empty or missing folder, or a non-dict model. Chameleon's errors pass through unwrapped: a missing template is `ValueError`, a missing model variable is `NameError`.
- A name that leaves the folder (an absolute path, a `..` out of it, a `package:path` spec) or names a folder is refused as `ValueError: Template not found`. The check is lexical, so a symlink inside the folder is followed. Never build the path from request data; map request values to names you wrote.
- `render_partial` is injected into the model only when the key is absent, so `render_partial(name, **request.params)` lets a request replace it. Pass named keyword arguments.
- Do not name a model value `encoding` (the package passes it to Chameleon; yours raises `TypeError`). `translate`, `target_language`, and `repeat` belong to Chameleon.
- Pass the returned `HTML` object into templates. Read `.html_text` only for a response body or an assertion; a plain `str` is escaped on insertion.
- Names are normalized (`./`, `//`, a `..` that stays inside, surrounding whitespace), so each file compiles once. A different case spelling on macOS or Windows still loads but is a separate cached template.
- With `auto_reload=True` a changed file recompiles on the next render; with the default `False`, template edits need a process restart.
- A partial that renders itself without a stopping condition raises `RecursionError`.
- Templates are TAL and METAL, not Jinja: `${ expr }`, `tal:repeat`, `tal:condition`, `tal:define`. There is no `{% %}` or `{ }`.

## Decision table

| Need | Use |
|------|-----|
| Insert a fragment in a template | `${ render_partial('shared/partials/x.pt', key=value) }` |
| Give every Pyramid template `render_partial` | `BeforeRender` subscriber setting `event['render_partial']` |
| Give a template `render_partial` in another framework | `return chameleon_partials.extend_model(model)` |
| Fragment as a string (HTMX response, email, test) | `render_partial(path, **model).html_text` |
| See template edits without a restart | `register_extensions(folder, auto_reload=True)` |
| Register a different folder in the same process | `register_extensions(folder, cache_init=False)` or reset `has_registered_extensions` |
| Let a request choose the fragment | `PARTIALS = {'card': 'shared/partials/card.pt'}` then `render_partial(PARTIALS[key], ...)` |

## API

- `register_extensions(template_folder: str, auto_reload: bool = False, cache_init: bool = True) -> None`: raises `PartialsException` for an empty or non-directory folder. Call once at startup.
- `render_partial(template_file: str, **template_data) -> HTML`: raises `PartialsException` before registration and `ValueError` for a missing, folder, or refused name; Chameleon's render errors propagate. Injects itself into the model when absent.
- `extend_model(model: dict | None) -> dict`: sets `model['render_partial']` (replacing any existing key) and returns the same dict; `None` gives a new dict; a non-dict raises `PartialsException`.
- `PartialsException(Exception)`: misconfiguration or misuse only.
- `HTML` (not in `__all__`): `html_text` holds the markup and `__html__()` returns it.

## Example output

```text
>>> render_partial('shared/partials/video_square.pt', video=v).html_text
'<div>\n    <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=abc123" target="_blank">\n        <img src="https://img.youtube.com/vi/abc123/maxresdefault.jpg"\n     class="img img-responsive "\n     alt="Talk Python"\n     title="Talk Python">\n    </a>\n    ...\n    <div class="views">12,345 views</div>\n</div>'
# The <img> came from the nested video_image.pt partial, inserted unescaped by video_square.pt.
>>> render_partial('shared/partials/missing.pt')
ValueError: Template not found: shared/partials/missing.pt.
>>> render_partial('x.pt')  # before register_extensions
PartialsException: You must call register_extensions() before this function can be used.
```

When a render fails, fix in this order: register the folder, get `render_partial` into the model, make the path relative to the registered folder, then supply every name the partial uses.

## Resources

- [Documentation](https://mkennedy.codes/docs/chameleon-partials/) (every page has a Markdown twin: swap `.html` for `.md`)
- [Getting started](https://mkennedy.codes/docs/chameleon-partials/user-guide/getting-started.html), [Writing partials](https://mkennedy.codes/docs/chameleon-partials/user-guide/writing-partials.html), [Testing](https://mkennedy.codes/docs/chameleon-partials/user-guide/testing.html), [Troubleshooting](https://mkennedy.codes/docs/chameleon-partials/user-guide/troubleshooting.html)
- [API reference](https://mkennedy.codes/docs/chameleon-partials/reference/), [llms.txt](https://mkennedy.codes/docs/chameleon-partials/llms.txt), [llms-full.txt](https://mkennedy.codes/docs/chameleon-partials/llms-full.txt)
- [Source](https://github.com/mikeckennedy/chameleon_partials) and the [example Pyramid app](https://github.com/mikeckennedy/chameleon_partials/tree/main/example)

title: Changelog
text:
[0.2.0] - 2026-06-10

Added

Google-style docstrings, complete type annotations, and runnable usage examples for the public API (register_extensions, render_partial, extend_model, PartialsException) and the internal HTML wrapper.
PEP 561 py.typed marker, so type checkers consume the package’s inline type annotations; the package checks clean under ty and pyrefly, which join the dev requirements.
Documentation site rendered from those docstrings with Great Docs, published at https://mkennedy.codes/docs/chameleon-partials/. Includes scripts/build_docs.py and scripts/serve_docs.py; the built site is committed in docs/, and great-docs joins the dev extra (skipped automatically on Python < 3.11).
Project URLs in the package metadata for the PyPI sidebar — Issues, Changelog, and Funding (GitHub Sponsors) — alongside the existing Homepage, Repository, and Documentation links.
Pyramid BeforeRender middleware pattern, documented in the README and wired into the example app, so views do not have to add render_partial to every model by hand.
Test suite (tests/test_rendering.py) covering bare renders, partials with data, layouts, nested (recursive) partials, and error conditions.
Pytest configuration ([tool.pytest.ini_options], testpaths = ["tests"]) so a bare pytest from the repo root runs only the package’s tests instead of erroring while collecting the standalone example/ app’s suite (which needs Pyramid and WebTest).
This changelog.



Changed

Packaging migrated from setup.py to a PEP 621 pyproject.toml. The version stays single-sourced in chameleon_partials/__init__.py and dependencies in requirements*.txt (read dynamically), so the built wheel is unchanged aside from added project URLs.
Raised the minimum supported Python from 3.6 to 3.9 (3.6-3.8 are end-of-life and match no supported Chameleon release). Trove classifiers now cover Python 3.9-3.14, and the development status is Production/Stable.



Fixed

register_extensions no longer marks the extension as registered when registration fails. The flag used to be set before the template folder was validated, so a failed call left the library flagged as registered and a later retry with the default cache_init=True silently did nothing. Failed registrations can now simply be retried. (Behavior change.)
extend_model’s type annotation now accepts None (Optional[Dict[str, Any]]), matching its documented and actual behavior.
Ruff’s target-version is now py39 to match requires-python (was py313), so Ruff won’t rewrite code into newer-only idioms that would break on Python 3.9.
README accuracy: the Pyramid startup snippet now imports Configurator, the listing snippet matches the example app’s template (span, not div), and several typos were corrected: “incredible easy”, “subtitle of author”, “them middleware”, and “veiws” (#2, thanks @hodgesd).

title: Troubleshooting
text:
This is a field guide. Each heading is an error message, or the symptom you see when there is no message, so you can search this page for the exact text in your terminal. Under each one: what happened, why, and what to do about it.
The first five come from chameleon_partials itself and arrive as PartialsException. They all mean the library was set up or called wrongly, and they are all quick to fix. Everything after that comes from Chameleon or Python and passes through unchanged, because the package deliberately never wraps another library’s errors.

PartialsException: You must call register_extensions() before this function can be used
render_partial ran before anyone told the library where the templates are. This is the classic first-request-in-a-new-project error. Move register_extensions to application startup, before the first request is served: in Pyramid, the main function that builds the WSGI app. In a test, add a fixture that registers the test template folder, as shown in Testing.


PartialsException: The template_folder must be specified
register_extensions was called with an empty string or None, usually from a setting that was never filled in. Pass the path to the templates folder, and build it from __file__ so the working directory cannot change the answer:
folder = (Path(__file__).parent / 'templates').as_posix()


PartialsException: The specified template folder must be a folder
The path exists in your head but not on disk, or it points at a file. Check the spelling and whether the path is meant to be absolute or relative. The failed call did not mark the library as registered, so once the path is right, a plain retry works. No flag to reset.


PartialsException: The model must be a dictionary
extend_model was handed something other than a dict or None. A common way to get here is returning a list or a model object from a view and wrapping that. Pass the view-model dictionary, or None to get a fresh one back.


ValueError: Template not found
render_partial could not turn the name into a regular file inside the registered folder. This is the most common error on this page, and it has five causes. Work through them in order:

The path is relative to the registered folder, not to the calling template. From inside shared/partials/a.pt, a sibling is shared/partials/b.pt, not b.pt and not ./b.pt. This is the cause nine times out of ten.
The name points at a folder rather than a file, for example shared/partials without the file name on the end.
The name reaches outside the registered folder: an absolute path, a .. that climbs out, or a package:path spec. These are refused on purpose. Move the file under the registered folder, or register a folder higher up.
The case does not match on Linux. Video_Square.pt and video_square.pt are different files there, even though macOS and Windows would cheerfully load either. This one tends to appear the first time the app runs in a container.
The registered folder is not the one you think, usually because an earlier register_extensions call pointed somewhere else and the second call was a no-op. See the next heading.



render_partial uses the wrong folder, or a second register_extensions is ignored
With the default cache_init=True, register_extensions does nothing once a previous call has succeeded. In an application that is the behaviour you want. In a test suite, or in a process that must switch folders, pass cache_init=False or set chameleon_partials.has_registered_extensions = False before registering again.


NameError: render_partial
Chameleon went looking for render_partial in the template’s model and found nothing. A partial always receives it, so this only happens in a page template, and it means the wiring step was skipped or did not take. In Pyramid, check that the module holding the BeforeRender subscriber sits inside a package that config.scan() covers; a subscriber in a file nobody imports is a subscriber that never registers. In other frameworks, make sure the view returns chameleon_partials.extend_model(model) and not just model.


NameError: some other name
A partial references a name that the render_partial call did not pass. Chameleon’s message shows the expression, the file, and the line, so the fix is usually obvious: add the keyword argument to the call, or give the partial a fallback with tal:define if the value is genuinely optional.


TypeError: render() got multiple values for keyword argument ‘encoding’
The model included a value called encoding. That name is already taken by the package’s own call into Chameleon. Rename the variable; charset or text_encoding both work.


The fragment shows up as escaped text
The page displays the markup literally, <div> and all. The value inserted into the template was a plain string, almost always html_text, instead of the HTML object that render_partial returns. Pass the object through to the template and read html_text only at the edge, where you need a real str: a response body, an email, a test assertion.


Edits to a template do not show up
You changed the file, refreshed, and nothing happened. Chameleon compiled the template once and is serving the compiled version. Register with auto_reload=True during development so it checks the file’s timestamp on each render. In production, leave it False and restart after deploying template changes.


RecursionError
A partial renders itself, directly or through a chain of other partials, with nothing to stop it. Add a tal:condition around the nested call that checks a depth counter or an empty children list, and pass that value down on each call.


IsADirectoryError, or a file outside the templates folder rendered
Both were possible in older releases: the directory error until 0.2.2, the outside file until 0.2.1. Upgrade. Current releases report a folder name or an outside path as ValueError: Template not found, and the containment check sees the name exactly as Chameleon’s loader does. The check is lexical, so a symlink inside the folder is still followed; keep symlinks out of the templates folder if that matters to you.

title: Getting started
text:
This page takes an app from nothing to a rendered fragment in four moves. It assumes a framework that already renders Chameleon templates, such as Pyramid with pyramid_chameleon, or FastAPI calling Chameleon directly. The snippets come from the demo video site, so the fragment we build is the YouTube thumbnail that every video card shares.

Move one: install
uv add chameleon-partials
# or
pip install chameleon-partials
Two spellings, and both matter. The distribution on PyPI is chameleon-partials with a hyphen. The module you import is chameleon_partials with an underscore. The package is pure Python and its only runtime dependency is Chameleon itself.


Move two: tell the library where the templates live
The library needs to know one thing before it can do anything: the root folder of your Chameleon templates. Tell it once, at startup, before any template renders:
from pathlib import Path

import chameleon_partials

folder = (Path(__file__).parent / 'templates').as_posix()
chameleon_partials.register_extensions(folder, auto_reload=True)
Build the path from __file__ rather than a relative string, so it works no matter which directory the process was launched from. Every partial you render later is named by its path relative to this folder, which is why this is the only place the folder ever appears.
auto_reload=True makes Chameleon check a template’s modification time on each render and recompile when it changed, so you can edit a fragment and refresh the browser. It costs a stat call per render, so leave it at the default False in production and restart on deploy.
In a Pyramid app this call belongs in the main function that builds the WSGI app. In FastAPI it goes at module level beside the app object, or in the lifespan startup. The registration is process-wide module state, so it wants single-threaded startup code, not a request handler.
One more thing worth knowing now rather than later: once a call to register_extensions has succeeded, calling it again does nothing. That is on purpose, so an app that initialises twice does not rebuild its loader, and it is exactly the behaviour a test suite needs to know about. Testing covers how to point tests at their own folder.


Move three: open the door for your templates
A template can only call render_partial if that name is in its model. Chameleon has no global namespace to drop it into, so you wire it once in whatever way your framework offers.
Pyramid has the nicest answer. A BeforeRender subscriber runs before every template render and can add names to the model. Put this file inside the package that config.scan() covers and forget about it:
# views/partials_middleware.py
from pyramid.events import BeforeRender, subscriber

import chameleon_partials


@subscriber(BeforeRender)
def add_global(event):
    event['render_partial'] = chameleon_partials.render_partial
Every view in the app now returns its model exactly as before, and every template can call render_partial.
Elsewhere, extend the model dictionary on its way out of the view:
model = {'videos': videos}
return chameleon_partials.extend_model(model)
extend_model adds the render_partial key to the dictionary you give it and returns that same dictionary. Hand it None and you get a fresh dictionary back.


Move four: write a fragment and render it
A partial is a plain Chameleon template holding a piece of HTML. No layout, no <html> element, no metal:define-macro. Here is the thumbnail, as it lives in the demo app:
<!-- templates/shared/partials/video_image.pt -->
<img src="https://img.youtube.com/vi/${ video.id }/maxresdefault.jpg"
     class="img img-responsive ${ ' '.join(classes or []) }"
     alt="${ video.title }"
     title="${ video.title }">
It uses two names, video and classes. Nothing in the file says where those come from, and that is the point: they come from whoever renders it. A folder named shared/partials/ is only a convention, but it is a good one, because six months from now you will want to know which .pt files are pages and which are pieces.
Now render it. From a page template, or from inside another partial, call render_partial in a ${ } expression. The first argument is the path relative to the registered folder, and the keyword arguments are the fragment’s model:
<a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=${ video.id }" target="_blank">
    ${ render_partial('shared/partials/video_image.pt', video=video, classes=[]) }
</a>
Reload the page and the thumbnail is there. Behind the scenes render_partial looked the file up in the registered folder, rendered it with video and classes in scope, and returned an HTML object rather than a string. Chameleon notices the object’s __html__ method and inserts the markup as is. Had the function returned a plain string, Chameleon would have escaped it and you would be looking at a literal <img on the page. That small wrapper is what makes the whole thing feel native.
Those four moves are the entire library. Everything else is the rulebook, and Writing partials is where it lives.

title: Testing
text:
Template code has a reputation for being hard to test, and it is mostly earned: you need a running app, a request, a session, and a browser-shaped tool to read the result. Partials sidestep all of that. render_partial is a function that takes a path and some keyword arguments and returns a string wrapped in an object. You can call it from a test the way you would call any other function, with no web framework in sight.
There is one thing to know first, and it is the reason this page exists.

The one-shot registration, and the fixture that tames it
register_extensions keeps its state in module globals, and with the default cache_init=True, a second call after a successful one is a no-op. In production that is a feature. In a test suite it is a trap: the first folder anyone registers wins for the rest of the session, and a test that registers a different folder will quietly keep rendering from the old one.
The fix is a fixture that registers the test folder and then clears the flag on the way out, so the next test starts clean:
from pathlib import Path

import pytest

import chameleon_partials


@pytest.fixture
def registered_extension():
    folder = (Path(__file__).parent / 'test_templates').as_posix()
    chameleon_partials.register_extensions(folder, auto_reload=True)
    yield
    chameleon_partials.has_registered_extensions = False
Resetting has_registered_extensions is all it takes. The next register_extensions call builds a fresh loader as if nothing had happened. Passing cache_init=False on every call works too, but the fixture keeps the knowledge in one place.
A registration that raised, say because the folder does not exist, never sets the flag in the first place. That means a failed call can simply be retried once the path is fixed, and it means a typo in a fixture path fails loudly rather than leaving a half-registered module behind.


Asserting on markup
With the fixture in place, a rendering test is three lines. Call the function, read html_text, look for the markup you expect:
def test_render_with_data(registered_extension):
    html = chameleon_partials.render_partial('render/with_data.pt', name='Sarah', age=32)
    assert '<span>Your name is Sarah and age is 32</span>' in html.html_text
Nested partials need nothing extra, because render_partial is injected into every partial’s model. A test that renders the video card has also exercised the thumbnail inside it, which is usually what you want: test the card people see, not the pieces in isolation.


Testing the promises about errors
The package makes two promises about errors, and tests can lean on both.
First, PartialsException means misuse and nothing else: rendering before registration, registering an empty or non-existent folder, or handing extend_model something that is not a dictionary. Second, everything Chameleon raises passes through untouched. A missing template is Chameleon’s ValueError, not a PartialsException, so code that already catches Chameleon’s errors keeps working when it starts rendering through partials:
def test_missing_template(registered_extension):
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match='Template not found'):
        chameleon_partials.render_partial('no-way.pt')


def test_not_registered():
    with pytest.raises(chameleon_partials.PartialsException):
        chameleon_partials.render_partial('doesnt-matter.pt')
The second test is the one place the fixture must be absent. It has to run either before any fixture has registered a folder, or after one has reset the flag, which the fixture above guarantees.


Testing through the framework
Unit tests on fragments catch most things, but they will not catch a BeforeRender subscriber that config.scan() never found. For that, one functional test through the real app is worth a dozen mocks. The demo app does it with WebTest in example/tests/test_functional.py: fetch the home page, assert that the thumbnail markup is in the body. If that passes, the subscriber ran, the layout rendered, the page filled the slot, the loop iterated, and two levels of partials did their job. Nothing in the package needs mocking; register the real template folder in the app factory exactly as production does.


auto_reload in tests
auto_reload=True tells Chameleon to check a template’s modification time on each render and recompile when it changed. A test that writes template files on the fly needs it. A suite over a fixed set of template files does not, and the default False saves a stat call per render. The fixture above turns it on, which costs nothing noticeable and means a test can edit a template mid-run if it ever needs to.

title: User Guide
text:
Every web app has a piece of HTML it cannot stop repeating. In the demo app that ships with this library it is a video card: a YouTube thumbnail, the channel name, and a view count. The card appears on the home page in a row of three. It appears again on the listing page, dozens of times. The first time you build it you copy the markup from one template into the other and move on, because that is what Tuesday afternoons are for.
Then the view count needs a thousands separator. You fix it on the home page, ship it, and a week later someone sends a screenshot of the listing page still showing 10302 views. Now there are two cards, and they will keep drifting apart for as long as the app lives.
Chameleon has no built-in answer to this. It has macros, which are good at layouts and clumsy at small reusable pieces with their own data. chameleon_partials adds one function, render_partial, that a template calls to drop a fragment in place and hand it a model:
<span class="video" tal:repeat="v videos">
    ${ render_partial('shared/partials/video_square.pt', video=v) }
</span>
The fragment is an ordinary Chameleon template living under a folder you register once at startup. It gets the keyword arguments as its model, it can call render_partial itself to pull in smaller fragments, and the markup it produces is inserted unescaped, so the page sees HTML rather than a string of angle brackets. The video card becomes one file, and the thousands separator gets fixed once.

Where to go next

Getting started takes an app from pip install to its first rendered fragment in four moves: install, register the folder, hand render_partial to your templates, and call it.
Writing partials is the rulebook. How a partial’s path resolves (this is the one rule everyone trips on), how the model gets in, nesting, loops, METAL layouts, rendering a fragment straight from Python for HTMX, and why the request must never choose the file.
Testing shows that partials are plain functions over plain files, which makes them pleasant to test, as long as you know about the one-shot registration.
Troubleshooting is a field guide to every error the package or Chameleon raises in normal use. Each heading is the message you will see, so you can search for it.
API reference holds the four public names with their full docstrings.

The example Pyramid app in the repository is the video site described above, and it is the source of every snippet in this guide: a BeforeRender subscriber, nested partials inside tal:repeat loops, and METAL layout inheritance, all working together in about a dozen files.

title: Chameleon Partials
text:
Overview
When building real-world web apps with Chameleon, it’s easy to end up with repeated HTML fragments. Just like organizing code for reuse, it would be ideal to reuse smaller sections of HTML template code. That’s what this library is all about.

title: Chameleon Partials
text:
Example
This project comes with a sample Pyramid application (see the example folder). This app displays videos that can be played on YouTube. The image, author subtitle, and view count are reused throughout the app. Here’s a visual:



Video image, author, and view count HTML reused across pages of the demo app


Check out the demo / example application to see it in action.

title: Chameleon Partials
text:
Installation
It’s just pip install chameleon-partials (or uv add chameleon-partials) and you’re all set with this pure Python package. It needs Python 3.10 or newer and depends only on Chameleon.

title: Chameleon Partials
text:
Usage
Using the library is incredibly easy. The first step is to register the partial method with Chameleon. Do this once at app startup:
from pathlib import Path

from pyramid.config import Configurator

import chameleon_partials


def main(_, **settings):
    """This function returns a Pyramid WSGI application."""
    with Configurator(settings=settings) as config:
        config.include('pyramid_chameleon')
        config.include('.routes')
        config.scan()

        # Register the extension for working with Chameleon.
        folder = (Path(__file__).parent / 'templates').as_posix()
        chameleon_partials.register_extensions(folder, auto_reload=True, cache_init=True)

    return config.make_wsgi_app()
Set auto_reload=True while developing so template edits show up without a restart, and leave it at the default False in production. Calling register_extensions again after it has succeeded does nothing, so repeated startup calls are safe (see Testing for pointing tests at their own folder).
Next, you define your main HTML (Chameleon) templates as usual. Then define your partial templates. I recommend locating and naming them accordingly:
├── templates
│   ├── errors
│   │   └── 404.pt
│   ├── home
│   │   ├── index.pt
│   │   └── listing.pt
│   └── shared
│       ├── _layout.pt
│       └── partials
│           ├── video_image.pt
│           └── video_square.pt
Notice the partials subfolder in the templates/shared folder.
The templates are just HTML fragments. Here is a stand-alone one for the YouTube thumbnail from the example app:
<img src="https://img.youtube.com/vi/${ video.id }/maxresdefault.jpg"
     class="img img-responsive ${ ' '.join(classes or []) }"
     alt="${ video.title }"
     title="${ video.title }">
Notice that an object called video and a list of classes are passed in as the model.
Templates can also be nested. Here is the whole single video fragment with the image as well as other info linking out to YouTube:
<div>
    <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=${ video.id }" target="_blank">
        ${ render_partial('shared/partials/video_image.pt', video=video, classes=[]) }
    </a>
    <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=${ video.id }" target="_blank"
       class="author">${ video.author }</a>
    <div class="views">${ "{:,}".format(video.views) } views</div>
</div>
Now you see the render_partial() method. It takes the subpath into the templates folder and any model data passed in as keyword arguments. The path is always relative to the registered folder, even when the call is inside another partial. It returns an HTML object that Chameleon inserts unescaped; read its html_text attribute when you need the string, for example in a test or an HTMX response.
We can finally generate the list of video blocks as follows:
<span class="video" tal:repeat="v videos">
    ${ render_partial('shared/partials/video_square.pt', video=v) }
</span>
This time, we reframe each item in the list from the outer template (called v) as the video model in the inner HTML section.

title: Chameleon Partials
text:
Choosing Partials Safely
Choose the partial in your code, never from request data. render_partial() refuses a name that would reach outside the registered template folder (an absolute path, a .. out of the folder, or a package:path spec), but a request that picks the fragment should still be mapped to a name you wrote rather than used to build the path:
PARTIALS = {'card': 'shared/partials/video_square.pt', 'row': 'shared/partials/video_row.pt'}
html = render_partial(PARTIALS[request.params['style']], video=video)
Pass the model as named keyword arguments too. Spreading a request’s parameters into it (render_partial(name, **request.params)) lets a parameter replace a name the template relies on, including render_partial itself.

title: Chameleon Partials
text:
The View Methods
In order to share the render_partial() function with your template, you’ll need to pass it along to the template with your model (dictionary).
If you are using the Pyramid web framework, you can add this file as middleware. Just drop it into your views folder:
## views/partials_middleware.py
from pyramid.events import subscriber, BeforeRender

import chameleon_partials


@subscriber(BeforeRender)
def add_global(event):
    event['render_partial'] = chameleon_partials.render_partial
For other frameworks using Chameleon (e.g. FastAPI), you can add render_partial to the resulting dictionary. We’ve built a simple function to keep this fool-proof:
chameleon_partials.extend_model(model)
Here’s a typical view method that uses render_partial, notice the use of extending the model before passing it to the template (the example app’s views skip this because the middleware above handles it):
@view_config(route_name='listing', renderer='demo_chameleon_partials:templates/home/listing.pt')
def listing(_):
    videos = video_service.all_videos()
    model = dict(videos=videos)
    return chameleon_partials.extend_model(model)
Again: If you are using Pyramid, use the middleware. Otherwise, use the extend_model() method or something similar to the middleware in your framework.

title: Chameleon Partials
text:
Testing
Partials are plain functions over plain files, so tests need no web framework. Register the test template folder in a fixture and reset the registration flag afterwards, because a second register_extensions() call is a no-op by default:
@pytest.fixture
def registered_extension():
    folder = (Path(__file__).parent / 'test_templates').as_posix()
    chameleon_partials.register_extensions(folder, auto_reload=True)
    yield
    chameleon_partials.has_registered_extensions = False


def test_render_with_data(registered_extension):
    html = chameleon_partials.render_partial('render/with_data.pt', name='Sarah', age=32)
    assert '<span>Your name is Sarah and age is 32</span>' in html.html_text
The Testing page covers the error contract: PartialsException is raised for misuse only, and Chameleon’s own errors (such as the ValueError for a missing template) pass through unchanged.

title: Chameleon Partials
text:
Troubleshooting
Every error you can hit in normal use, with its cause and fix, is on the Troubleshooting page: rendering before registration, Template not found, NameError: render_partial, markup that shows up escaped, and template edits that do not appear.

title: register_extensions()
text:
Register chameleon_partials with Chameleon so partials can be rendered.


Usage
Source


register_extensions(template_folder, auto_reload=False, cache_init=True)


Call this once during application startup, before any template is rendered. It builds a Chameleon PageTemplateLoader rooted at template_folder and stores it in module-level state that render_partial uses to locate templates. Registration is process-wide and is not guarded by a lock, so call it from normal single-threaded startup code rather than from concurrent request handlers.


Parameters


template_folder: str

Path to the root folder containing your Chameleon templates (with a partials subfolder by convention). Must be an existing directory. Partials are later looked up by path relative to this folder.

auto_reload: bool = False

When True, Chameleon reloads a template from disk whenever the file changes. Useful during development; leave False in production.

cache_init: bool = True

When True (the default), calling this again after a previous successful registration is a no-op, which makes repeated startup calls safe. Pass False to force re-registration, for example to point at a different template folder in tests.





Raises


 PartialsException

If template_folder is empty or is not an existing directory.





Examples
import chameleon_partials

# At startup; use auto_reload=True while developing.
chameleon_partials.register_extensions('path/to/templates', auto_reload=True)

title: API Reference
text:
The complete public API of chameleon_partials: register the extension, render partial templates, share render_partial with your view models, and handle errors.


Setup

Register chameleon_partials with Chameleon. Call this once at application startup.


register_extensions()

Register chameleon_partials with Chameleon so partials can be rendered.




Rendering partials

Render partial templates and expose render_partial to your view models.


render_partial()

Render a partial template to an HTML fragment.

extend_model()

Add render_partial to a view model so templates can call it.




Exceptions

Errors raised by the library.


PartialsException

Raised when chameleon_partials is configured or used incorrectly.
